retrieved.title: ED triage guidelines
retrieved.text:
## 2.4 Caffeine withdrawal

Caffeine withdrawal headache usually begins 12 to 24 hours after a sharp cut in intake and can last two to nine days. Gradual tapering, fluids and simple painkillers are usually enough; it rarely needs emergency care.

Ask about recent changes in coffee, tea, energy drinks and cola. Patients often do not connect a new headache with cutting back a week earlier. A slower taper (reducing by about a quarter every few days) prevents most withdrawal headaches.

retrieved.title: Moot court notes
retrieved.text:
Moot court notes: "This house would adopt a nationwide four-day work week" V. Hale, for the Meridian Bar Society exhibition debate. Private notes.

¶ 1. Expect the opposition to say the evidence base is narrow. Concede scope early, then shift the burden: the status quo is also a policy and has to justify itself.

¶ 2. Historical anchor: the Meridian Working Hours Act 1931 made the two-day weekend the default. It gave agriculture and shipping a ten-year transition and exempted continuous services.

¶ 3. Continuous-coverage sectors already run on shift rules under Part IV of the Working Time Code: rest periods, a cap on consecutive shifts, and averaging over a reference period. A shorter standard week sits inside that structure.

¶ 4. Phase-in precedent: sector-by-sector timetables, collective agreements first, the public sector as model employer. Courts have upheld staged duties where the end point is clear.

messages.content: The motion before us: This house would tax sugary drinks. Speaking for the proposition, Amara Okafor, emergency physician and public-health researcher; speaking against, Victor Hale, constitutional litigator.

Taxes change what people actually buy — that's the point. Sugary drinks are cheap, everywhere, and marketed hardest to kids and low-income neighborhoods, so the costs land on all of us through diabetes, amputations, dialysis. A tax cuts consumption, nudges reformulation, and raises revenue we can put back into those same communities. This isn't about banning anything; your soda stays on the shelf, just priced honestly. Where's the harm in making the price tell the truth?

Three points, and I will be uncharacteristically brief on each. First, definition: a tax is not a nudge, it is a coercion dressed in arithmetic, and this house should be honest that it proposes to make the poor pay more for the same bottle. Second, regressivity: the levy lands hardest on those with the least, while the comfortable absorb it without a shrug. Third, efficacy: substituting one beverage for another is a choice, and a price signal does not create the education, the time, or the alternatives it presumes. We can debate each.

Proposition argued that a sugary-drink tax cuts consumption, spurs reformulation, and funds affected communities; Opposition argued it coerces, hits the poor hardest, and presumes alternatives that price alone cannot create. We now move to closing statements.

Victor calls the price tag coercion, but every cheap soda already carries a hidden bill — paid later, in emergency rooms, by the same families. Regressivity cuts both ways: the disease burden is regressive too. No, a tax alone won't fix everything; it's one lever, paired with the revenue going back into those communities. Price reminds us of the cost. That honesty is the stronger case.

Kai, the single question left open is this: when a government raises the price of a lawful good, does it cure the harm or merely relocate the burden? My colleague answers that the disease bill is regressive too, and I grant it. But granting a harm exists is not the same as proving your instrument reaches it; a levy on a bottle taxes the purchase, not the outcome. Define your terms. The motion says tax; it does not say cure. On the record as it stands, the price has been made to speak, and what it says is arithmetic, not health. The house should decline the motion.
Thank you, Amara Okafor and Victor Hale, for your arguments on the motion that this house would tax sugary drinks. The arbiter is now weighing the arguments.
